1226.title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
1226.hook: a teacher's hand curled closed, a student's promises, and the book that came of one of them
1226.howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, the Sri Bhashya is studied with a teacher, often alongside its later commentaries, and students learn its method: set out the opposing view in full, then answer it from the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Alvar hymns: ten verses that led Nathamuni to a thousand, and a lost Tamil Veda handed back, through a line of teachers that would reach Ramanuja.
screen: `THE TAMIL VEDA, FOUND AGAIN.` · `TODAY: RAMANUJA'S BOOK.`

segments.voice: A hand, curled closed. The Sri Vaishnava tradition says that when the young Ramanuja hurried to meet the great teacher Yamuna, he arrived too late. Yamuna had died, and some fingers of his hand were curled tight, as if holding on to something. Those around him read them as wishes left undone. Ramanuja stood by the body and made promises aloud, and with each one, the story says, a finger straightened. One of those promises was a book: the Sri Bhashya.
screen: `A HAND, CURLED CLOSED.` → `A PROMISE FOR EACH FINGER.` → `ONE OF THEM WAS A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The promise was a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and the student kept it. The Brahma Sutras are tiny, packed lines, too short to understand alone. A bhashya is a commentary that opens them up, line by line. And the Sri Bhashya argues in the open. Again and again Ramanuja sets out the opposing view first, in full, as if a sharp rival were sitting across from him, and only then answers. Indian commentaries call that the purvapaksha, the prior view. Among his opponents are other Vedanta teachers, and he gives their arguments at length before replying. What does he argue for? That the Brahman of the Upanishads is a person, Narayana, Vishnu, full of every good quality and free of every fault. That the world is real. That each self is real, and never apart from God. And that the Upanishads, the Gita and the Alvars' devotion are saying one thing, not several. Theology, in this book, means thinking hard about a God you can also love. Over the next days, a few of its pieces, one at a time.
screen: `A PROMISE TO A TEACHER'S HAND.` · `BHASHYA: OPENING A TINY LINE.` · `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `A GOD TO THINK ABOUT, AND LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one disagreement you're carrying, at home or at work; small is fine. In your head, say the other person's side as well as you can, in full, as if you were defending it, and stay there a few breaths before your own view comes back. Notice whether anything shifts; if you pray, rest in the name you pray to as you sit with both.
Vaishnava theology. Today, Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya: a promise to a teacher, a commentary that states the other view first, and a God to think about and love.
screen: `VAISHNAVA THEOLOGY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). A promise at a teacher's side became a book that hears the other side first. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1227.title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
1227.hook: one Upanishad sentence says what the self is not, and then what it is, and Ramanuja builds on holding both halves
1227.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas study the Sri Bhashya's reading of nirguna with a teacher, and in worship they praise Vishnu and Lakshmi through their qualities, in hymns, names and stotras that list the Lord's good qualities one by one.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday opened Vaishnava theology with Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, the book that states the other view first.
screen: `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `TODAY: WITHOUT, AND WITH.`

segments.voice: Free from evil. Free from old age. Free from death, from grief, from hunger, from thirst. That's how the Chandogya Upanishad begins describing the self worth seeking. A long run of withouts. And then, in the same breath, the sentence turns. Whose desires are real. Whose resolves come true. Suddenly there's someone there: someone who wants, and whose wanting is never empty. One sentence, two halves, a no and a yes. Some readers lean on the first half. Ramanuja says you have to keep both.
screen: `FREE FROM EVIL, AGE, DEATH, GRIEF.` → `THEN: WHOSE DESIRES ARE REAL.` → `A NO AND A YES.`

segments.voice: The Upanishads sometimes call Brahman nirguna, without qualities. Other passages pile qualities on: all-knowing, all-powerful, the source of joy. How do you read a text that seems to say both? Advaita teachers, in Shankara's line, read the withouts as the highest truth, and the qualities as true from where people stand, a lower vantage. Ramanuja, in the Sri Bhashya, reads it another way. Without qualities, he says, means without bad qualities: no evil, no decay, no limit, no lack. And the qualities the texts praise, knowledge, power, compassion, beauty, are fully real in Brahman. So the no and the yes aren't two levels. They're one portrait drawn from both sides: everything wrong ruled out, everything good affirmed. Sri Vaishnava teachers call Brahman an ocean of auspicious qualities. That's why the Chandogya sentence matters so much to him: it shows the pattern inside a single line, and neither half cancels the other. For Ramanuja, this has a human side. A God with every good quality and no flaw is someone you can bring a grief to, or sing to, as the Alvars did. His theology and their devotion meet right here. Both schools argue carefully from the same Upanishads, and both have their reasons; this is a chance to hear Ramanuja clearly, not to rank them.
screen: `NIRGUNA: WITHOUT QUALITIES.` · `WITHOUT BAD QUALITIES.` · `AN OCEAN OF GOOD QUALITIES.` · `SOMEONE YOU CAN TALK TO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love. First the withouts: for a few breaths, set down every complaint you have about them, what they forgot, what annoys you. Then the yes: name quietly the good that's really in them, their patience, their laugh, the way they show up; if you pray, turn the same no and yes toward the name you pray to.
Vaishnava theology. Today, without qualities read as without bad qualities, and an ocean of good ones: a no and a yes in one portrait.

1228.title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
1228.hook: oil poured from a jar falls in one thread without a break, and Ramanuja says that is what knowing God looks like
1228.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas cultivate steady remembrance of Vishnu through daily worship, recitation of his names and of the Alvar hymns, and quiet meditation, and teachers point to Ramanuja's image of oil poured in an unbroken stream.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, Ramanuja read without qualities as without bad qualities: a no and a yes in one portrait.
screen: `A NO AND A YES.` · `TODAY: A THREAD OF OIL.`

segments.voice: Tip a jar of oil, slowly, over a bowl. It doesn't splash or scatter. It falls in one thin, glossy thread, unbroken from the lip of the jar to the bowl below. Ramanuja reaches for that thread in the opening pages of the Sri Bhashya, when he asks a plain question. The Upanishads promise freedom to the one who knows Brahman. But what kind of knowing? Reading a sentence and nodding? Understanding it once, on a good afternoon? His answer is the thread of oil.
screen: `OIL FALLS IN ONE THREAD.` → `WHAT KIND OF KNOWING?` → `FOLLOW THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: The Upanishads use more than one word for this knowing: know, meditate, worship. Ramanuja argues they mean the same thing, and that it isn't a one-time flash of understanding. It's meditation that keeps going, a remembering of God that doesn't break, like oil poured in a steady stream. His key phrase comes from the Chandogya Upanishad: when one's food, the things taken in, is pure, the mind becomes pure; when the mind is pure, remembrance becomes firm; and with firm remembrance, every knot comes loose. Dhruva smriti: firm, steady remembrance. Then a step further. Remembered steadily enough, he says, it becomes so vivid that it's like seeing. And remembrance that is like seeing, and full of love, is what the Upanishads call knowing. That's bhakti. So for Ramanuja, devotion isn't a softer path beside knowledge. It's what knowledge becomes when it doesn't stop. One more turn. The Katha Upanishad says the self isn't gained by teaching or cleverness, but by the one it chooses. Who gets chosen? Ramanuja answers: the one who has become dearest, through this unbroken loving remembrance. Knowing, loving and being chosen run together, like one thread. The Alvars sang this; Ramanuja argues it, line by line.
screen: `KNOW, MEDITATE, WORSHIP: ONE THING.` · `LIKE OIL POURED, UNBROKEN.` · `SO STEADY IT'S LIKE SEEING.` · `KNOWING THAT DOESN'T STOP IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to hold in mind: a name you pray to, a face you love, or simply the breath. Let attention flow toward it slowly and evenly, like oil from a tipped jar. When it breaks, don't scold yourself; just tip the jar again and let the thread start over. If you pray, let the thread be the name you pray to.
Vaishnava theology. Today, knowing God as dhruva smriti: steady remembrance, poured like oil, so vivid it's like seeing, and full of love.

1229.title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
1229.hook: "I slept well": a sentence everyone says at breakfast becomes evidence in Ramanuja's argument about what awareness is
1229.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava students meet this argument in the Sri Bhashya's long opening section, studied with a teacher, where Ramanuja sets out the Advaita view in full and answers it; Advaita students study the replies made from their side.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, knowing God became a thread of oil: steady remembrance, so vivid it's like seeing.
screen: `A THREAD OF OIL.` · `TODAY: THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Breakfast. Someone asks how you slept, and you say, I slept well. Simple. But stop on it for a second. In deep sleep you weren't thinking, weren't dreaming, weren't aware of the room. So who slept well? And how does that someone know? Ramanuja uses exactly this ordinary sentence in the Sri Bhashya, in a long argument about what consciousness is, and whether there's a someone inside it. The breakfast table, it turns out, is a good place to do theology.
screen: `I SLEPT WELL.` → `WHO SLEPT, AND WHO KNOWS?` → `THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Advaita teachers, in Shankara's line, say the deepest reality is pure consciousness, with no owner and no object, and that the sense of I is laid over it, like a snake seen on a rope. Ramanuja sets that view out at length, then answers it. Every awareness, he says, has two features: it belongs to someone, and it shows something. I know the cup. I see the light. Awareness with no knower and nothing known isn't anything anyone has met. Then the breakfast line. On waking and saying I slept well, he argues, the I was there all along; it simply wasn't knowing much. So the self is a real knower, not a mask over knowing. To hold both, he uses a lamp. A lamp is bright in itself, and it also has light that spreads out from it into the room. The light is real, and it's the lamp's. In the same way, the self is conscious by nature, and it has consciousness that reaches out toward things. In bondage that reach is narrowed, like light behind a shutter. In freedom it opens wide. Advaita teachers answer him in turn, and both schools keep reading. For Ramanuja, the point is this: there's a someone in your awareness, real enough to love and to be loved.
screen: `AWARENESS BELONGS TO SOMEONE.` · `AND IT SHOWS SOMETHING.` · `THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.` · `NARROWED, THEN OPENED WIDE.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on one sound in the room, and notice both that there's a sound and that it's being heard. Then let attention widen, the way light spreads, to every sound at once, and narrow it again to one. Through all of it, notice the one who is noticing; if you pray, rest that noticing in the name you pray to.
Vaishnava theology. Today, Ramanuja's lamp: a self that is conscious by nature, with a light of awareness that narrows and opens wide.

1230.title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
1230.hook: a brass pot polished before a festival doesn't get a new shine; the old one comes back, and Ramanuja says freedom works the same way
1230.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas describe liberation, moksha, as the self reaching Vishnu's own realm, Vaikuntha, and serving him there forever in joy; teachers study Ramanuja's comments on the last section of the Brahma Sutras for this teaching.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, Ramanuja's lamp: a self that's conscious by nature, its light narrowed in bondage and opened wide in freedom.
screen: `THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.` · `TODAY: THE SHINE COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The night before a festival, someone sits on the floor with the family's old brass pot, a lemon, some ash or tamarind, and a cloth. The pot has gone dull and brown. Rub, rinse, rub. Slowly it glows. Nobody added gold. Nothing new went in. The shine was the brass all along, under a film of time and smoke. Ramanuja reaches the last part of the Brahma Sutras, where the question is what happens to a self when it's finally free. Does it vanish? Does it turn into something else? His answer looks a lot like that pot on the floor.
screen: `THE OLD BRASS POT.` → `NOTHING NEW WENT IN.` → `WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A SELF IS FREE?`

segments.voice: The Chandogya Upanishad says the freed self, reaching the highest light, appears in its own form. The Brahma Sutra picks up that phrase, and Ramanuja leans hard on the word own. Freedom isn't the self getting a new nature; it's the self's real nature showing, the way the brass's shine shows. Its awareness, narrowed by karma, opens fully. It's free of evil, free of death and grief, with desires that come true, the same marks the Upanishad gave to the highest self. So does the freed self dissolve into God, like a drop into the sea? Not in Ramanuja's reading. The self stays a self. It knows Brahman directly, and experiences itself as inseparable from him, the way a body belongs to its soul. It shares Brahman's joy fully. But the Brahma Sutra draws one line, and Ramanuja keeps it: the freed self shares in everything except the running of the world. Creating, holding up and dissolving the universe stays with the Lord alone. Freed selves don't become rival gods. They're near enough to share every joy, and still themselves, still loving. For Sri Vaishnavas, freedom isn't the end of the relationship. It's the relationship with nothing in the way. Other schools of Vedanta describe freedom differently, and each reads these same sutras with care.
screen: `IT APPEARS IN ITS OWN FORM.` · `NOTHING NEW, ONLY UNCOVERED.` · `STILL A SELF, NEVER APART.` · `EVERYTHING EXCEPT RUNNING THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing in you that's gone dull lately: patience, humor, generosity, attention. Don't try to make it new; picture the film over it, tiredness, hurry, an old hurt, and on each out-breath let a little of it come away. Notice what was there all along, and if you pray, hold that shine toward the name you pray to.
Vaishnava theology. Today, freedom as the self appearing in its own form: uncovered, still itself, near God, sharing every joy except running the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, freedom was brass polished back to its own shine: a self still itself, sharing every joy except running the world.
screen: `THE SHINE COMES BACK.` · `TODAY: WHY MAKE A WORLD?`

segments.voice: A child's question, and a philosopher's too: if God already has everything, why make anything? People act because they lack something. They cook because they're hungry, work because the rent is due, build because the roof leaks. A being who lacks nothing has no reason to lift a finger. So either God needed the world, which would mean God wasn't complete, or the world has no reason at all. The Brahma Sutra raises this objection itself, plainly, as a problem for anyone who says Brahman made the world. Then it answers in a handful of words, and on this last day with the Sri Bhashya, Ramanuja unpacks them.
screen: `IF GOD HAS EVERYTHING, WHY MAKE ANYTHING?` → `WE ACT BECAUSE WE LACK.` → `THE SUTRA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The sutra's answer: it is only lila, play, as in the world. Ramanuja gives the picture. A great king who already rules everything, who wants for nothing, still plays a game with a ball, just for the joy of it. Nobody says he's playing because he's short of something. So too, he says, the Lord brings forth the world, holds it up and draws it back, as play: not from need, but from fullness. For Ramanuja the world is real, and it's held close: the world and every self are like the Lord's body, as yesterday's lesson put it. So this play isn't a trick or a dream. It's real, it's close, and it rests in someone who is joy itself. Look back across the week with him. A book that states the other view first. Without qualities read as without bad ones. Knowing as a thread of oil that becomes love. A lamp and its light. A self freed into its own shine. And today, a world made from fullness, as play. That's Vaishnava theology in a few strokes: careful argument, all of it in service of a God the Alvars sang to. Next, the same Brahma Sutras open again, read through another great commentator, Shankara, with jnana, knowing, at the center.
screen: `ONLY PLAY, AS IN THE WORLD.` · `A KING WHO PLAYS BALL.` · `FROM FULLNESS, NOT NEED.` · `A REAL WORLD, HELD CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Notice how much of today has run on lack: something to fix, something to get, something to finish, and let that be there. Then, for a few breaths, notice what's already enough: the breath arriving on its own, the floor holding you, light in the room. Let the breath move as if it were play, not work; if you pray, rest in the name you pray to, and in the world held close.
Vaishnava theology. Today, lila: a world made not from need but from fullness, as play, real and held close by the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the days on Vaishnava theology, reading the Brahma Sutra with Ramanuja: a world made from fullness, as play.
screen: `VAISHNAVA THEOLOGY: RAMANUJA'S READING.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: Late afternoon on a beach. Something flashes in the wet sand, and a kid runs for it, shouting that it's silver. It isn't. It's the inside of a shell, catching the light. For a few seconds, though, the silver was completely real to that kid. The running was real. The shout was real. Nothing in the sand changed when the mistake was seen. Only the seeing changed. That little scene is a Vedanta teaching example, and Shankara reaches for it before he has commented on a single line of the Brahma Sutra. Last week was the Brahma Sutra with Ramanuja. Now its opening pages, with Shankara, and his word: jnana.
screen: `SILVER IN THE SAND.` → `IT WAS A SHELL.` → `ONLY THE SEEING CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Jnana means knowing, knowledge. In this tradition it also names a whole way: freedom that comes through knowing, rather than through doing more. Shankara's commentary opens with a preface before the first sutra. He sets two things side by side: the one who knows, the I, and everything that can be known, the this. They are as opposed, he says, as darkness and light. Neither can be the other. And yet everyone mixes them up, all the time, without trying. I am tall. I am tired. I am going. This is mine. The knower takes on the features of the known, and the known borrows the life of the knower. He calls the mix-up adhyasa, placing one thing on another, like silver placed on shell, or one moon seen as two by a tired eye. Then something bold: ordinary life runs on this mix-up. Everyday ways of knowing, even the rules for ritual action, all work inside it. He isn't mocking daily life; he's describing where it stands. And the Upanishads, he says, are studied to undo the mix-up, not by adding a new experience, but by knowing. That knowing is jnana. Not every Vedanta teacher accepts this preface. Ramanuja argues against it at length in his own commentary, and his followers read the same sutras another way. For the next few days, Shankara makes his case through the first four lines.
screen: `JNANA: FREEDOM THROUGH KNOWING.` · `THE I AND THE THIS.` · `ADHYASA: SILVER ON THE SHELL.` · `THE TEXTS STUDIED TO UNDO IT.`

segments.voice: Notice one sensation, maybe tiredness, maybe warmth in the hands, and hear the sentence the mind makes about it: I am tired. Then, gently, say it another way inside: tiredness is being noticed. Don't argue with either sentence; just feel the small difference between them, and if you pray, rest in that noticing as your prayer.
Jnana. Knowing, and the way of freedom through knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that undoes the mix-up of the I and the this.
